narrative:
The 2018 Minnesota Twins never quite found the footing they needed to build on their surprising 2017 Wild Card appearance. Opening Day was an omen: Fernando Rodney, the mercurial closer the team had brought in to anchor the bullpen, surrendered a home run to Adam Jones on March 29 to set a tone that would echo all season. April was a disaster, the team stumbling to an 8-14 record as the bullpen leaked runs at an alarming rate. Bright moments existed — Max Kepler's clutch home runs, Eddie Rosario's grand slam, Miguel Sanó's emerging power — but they were consistently undermined by late-inning collapses and defensive blunders that became a signature of this roster's ceiling.

May and June offered a faint glimpse of what this team could be. The offense showed flashes of life through Sanó, Logan Morrison, and a memorable three-run blast from Eduardo Escobar on June 5 that swung a game decisively. Ehire Adrianza's unlikely grand slam on June 12 typified the unpredictable, if often inconsistent, offense. But the bullpen remained a house of cards. Ryan Pressly was victimized twice in quick succession, and Berríos absorbed a crushing grand slam late in June against the Cubs. The team finished May and June a combined 26-29, close enough to .500 to tease but never truly threatening.

July was the team's best month, and it came with genuine drama. Rosario's walk-off double against Boston on July 27 was the season's highest single positive swing, a moment of pure electricity at Target Field. Robbie Grossman belted a grand slam on July 2 to spark the run, and Kepler contributed a clutch hit-by-pitch that plated a critical run on July 25. The Twins went 14-13 in July, their best month, but the window slammed shut almost immediately as Fernando Rodney and the bullpen continued to torch late leads against the Red Sox in the same series that produced Rosario's heroics.

August and September were a slow fade. The Twins went a combined 29-27 in those final two months — respectable, even encouraging in spots — but any playoff hope had long since evaporated. Joe Mauer's rare home run on August 17 provided a feel-good moment, and Willians Astudillo's September blast reminded fans of the franchise's future depth. But a 78-84 finish told the real story: a rotation that couldn't quite carry the load, a bullpen that surrendered too many games, and an offense that ranked among the league's middle tier. This was a transitional season — competitive enough to avoid embarrassment, but not good enough to matter in October.

chapters.title: Opening Wounds
chapters.description: A brutal April exposes the Twins' bullpen vulnerabilities right from Opening Day, as Fernando Rodney and the relief corps doom an otherwise spirited lineup.

chapters.title: Glimmers in the Grind
chapters.description: May brings scattered offensive heroics from Morrison, Garver, and Sanó, offering hope even as the team hovers frustratingly near .500.

chapters.title: June's Mixed Signals
chapters.description: Escobar's three-run blast and Adrianza's unlikely grand slam give the Twins emotional wins in June, but bullpen collapses and a Berríos grand-slam disaster prevent any real momentum.

chapters.title: July's Best Days
chapters.description: The Twins post their best monthly record behind Rosario's walk-off double, Grossman's grand slam, and Kepler's clutch hit-by-pitch, briefly making them look like a dangerous club.

chapters.title: Fading Into Fall
chapters.description: August and September produce respectable baseball but no playoff chase, with Mauer's home run and Astudillo's surprise blast serving as bittersweet highlights of a season going through the motions.
